body.statement: For every \(k\ge0\) and \(n\ge2k+4\), \(d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{k,n})=2^{k+1}\) and therefore \[D_k(n)=2^{k+1}.\] One original coefficient \(e^{\star}\) separates all branches on a nonempty Zariski-open covariance set.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(d=k+1\) and \(n_0=2d+2=2k+4\).  We first treat the graph on the \(n_0\) displayed vertices in \(\mathrm{def:attaining\mbox{-}family}\).  It has \(3d\) directed arrows.  Its supplied set \(T\) contains the \(2d\) arrows out of \(0\) and the arrow \(P_1\to h\), so
\[
 |T|=2d+1=n_0-1,
 \qquad
 D\setminus T=\{P_i\to h:2\leq i\leq d\},
 \qquad
 |D\setminus T|=d-1=k.
\]
Every nonroot vertex has exactly one incoming arrow in \(T\), and every vertex is reached from \(0\).  Thus \(T\) is a rooted spanning arborescence.  The directed order with \(0\) first, then all \(P_i,Q_i\), and then \(h\), is topological, and \(e^{\star}=P_1\to h\) is an arrow.  Hence \(\mathrm{def:graph\mbox{-}class}\) gives
\[
 (G^{\star}_{k,n_0},T,e^{\star})\in\mathcal G_{n_0,k}.
\tag{1}
\]

We construct a regular covariance fiber.  Choose \(h_i\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb Q\) such that \(b_i^2>4h_i\), put \(H_0=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_d)\), and let \(H\) be a rational symmetric positive-definite matrix, sufficiently close to \(H_0\), whose diagonal remains \((h_1,\ldots,h_d)\).  The additional generic requirement on \(H\) used below is compatible with an arbitrarily small such perturbation.  In the vertex order \((0,P_1,\ldots,P_d,Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,h)\), prescribe
\[
 \Sigma^{\star}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&0&0&1\\
 0&H&H&0\\
 0&H&C_0I_d&b\\
 1&0&b^{\mathsf T}&M
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad b=(b_1,\ldots,b_d)^{\mathsf T}.
\tag{2}
\]
Choose the rational number \(C_0\) so that \(C_0I_d-H\succ0\).  The Schur complement of \(H\) in
\(
 \left(\begin{smallmatrix}H&H\\H&C_0I_d\end{smallmatrix}\right)
\)
is \(C_0I_d-H\), so the principal block indexed by \(P,Q\) is positive definite.  After adjoining the independent \(0\)-coordinate, choose the rational number \(M\) larger than the corresponding final Schur-complement threshold.  These two Schur-complement inequalities prove
\[
 \Sigma^{\star}\succ0.
\tag{3}
\]

Write
\[
 a_i=\lambda_{0P_i},\qquad c_i=\lambda_{0Q_i},\qquad
 z_i=\lambda_{P_i h},\qquad z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad x=-Hz.
\]
The missing pairs in this family are \(P_i\leftrightarrow Q_i\), \(P_i\leftrightarrow h\), and \(Q_i\leftrightarrow h\), for \(1\leq i\leq d\); all other pairs are allowed by \(B\).  Substitution of (2) into the residual formula \(F_{ij}\) gives, respectively,
\[
 0=-a_i-(Hz)_i,
 \qquad
 0=b_i-c_i-(Hz)_i,
 \qquad
 0=h_i+a_ic_i.
\tag{4}
\]
Because \(H\) is invertible, (4) is equivalent to
\[
 a_i=x_i,qquad c_i=x_i+b_i,qquad
 x_i^2+b_ix_i+h_i=0\quad(1\leq i\leq d),
 \qquad z=-H^{-1}x.
\tag{5}
\]
The discriminant of the \(i\)-th quadratic is \(b_i^2-4h_i>0\).  Thus each quadratic has exactly two distinct real roots and (5) has exactly \(2^d\) real solutions.  Under the invertible change from \(z\) to \(x\), elimination of the two linear groups in (4) shows that the residual Jacobian is nonsingular precisely when
\[
 \det(H)\prod_{i=1}^d(2x_i+b_i)\ne0.
\tag{6}
\]
Both factors in (6) are nonzero at every solution, because \(H\succ0\) and
\((2x_i+b_i)^2=b_i^2-4h_i>0\).  Hence all \(2^d\) points are reduced.
For each of them, defining \(\Omega=(I_{n_0}-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{\star}(I_{n_0}-\Lambda)\) makes the equations in (4) exactly the required missing-bidirected zeros.  Acyclicity makes \(I_{n_0}-\Lambda\) invertible, and (3) then gives \(\Omega\succ0\) by congruence.  Thus every displayed point is a support-valid real positive-definite source lift.

We now choose \(H\) so that the original coefficient \(z_1=\lambda_{e^{\star}}\) separates them.  At \(H=H_0\), two branches with different first quadratic roots have different values \(z_1=-x_1/h_1\).  If two branches have the same first root but vectors \(x\ne x'\), choose \(j>1\) with \(x_j\ne x'_j\) and set
\[
 H(s)=H_0+s(E_{1j}+E_{j1}).
\]
Differentiating \(-H(s)^{-1}x\) at \(s=0\) gives
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{ds}\bigl(z_1(x)-z_1(x')\bigr)\right|_{s=0}
 =\frac{x_j-x'_j}{h_1h_j}\ne0.
\tag{7}
\]
Consequently, for every pair of branches, equality of their \(z_1\)-values is a proper algebraic condition on the off-diagonal entries of \(H\).  There are finitely many pairs.  The complement of their union is dense in a Euclidean neighborhood of \(H_0\), and rational matrices are dense there.  We may therefore choose the rational \(H\) used in (2) to preserve positive definiteness and (6) while making all \(2^d\) values of \(z_1\) distinct.

It remains to transfer this regular specialized fiber to the generic source-prime fiber and to rule out additional generic branches.  Let \(A_i,C_i,Z\) denote the multihomogeneous degree markers for the blocks \((a_i)\), \((c_i)\), and \((z_1,\ldots,z_d)\), of respective sizes \(1,1,d\).  The residual for \(P_i,Q_i\) has block degrees bounded by \(A_i+C_i\); those for \(P_i,h\) and \(Q_i,h\) have block degrees bounded by \(A_i+Z\) and \(C_i+Z\).  Therefore the coefficient in \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\) is
\[
 \left[\left(\prod_{i=1}^d A_iC_i\right)Z^d\right]
 \prod_{i=1}^d(A_i+C_i)(A_i+Z)(C_i+Z)=2^d.
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, for each \(i\), exactly two selections produce \(A_iC_iZ\): choose \(A_i,Z,C_i\), or choose \(C_i,A_i,Z\), from the three factors in their displayed order.  Thus every zero-dimensional generic fiber has at most \(2^d\) points counted with multiplicity.  This count is made on the original polynomial residual system and therefore neither inverts a directed-coordinate denominator nor discards a zero-over-zero solution.

For completeness, we prove dominance and the lower degree directly.  There are exactly \(3d\) missing-bidirected residuals and \(3d\) directed coefficients.  If \(N=n_0=2d+2\), then
\[
 |D|+|B|+|V|
 =3d+\left\{\binom N2-3d\right\}+N
 =\frac{N(N+1)}2.
\tag{9}
\]
By \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\), the incidence space is integral and has this source dimension.  At any of the \(2^d\) points above, replace the covariance coordinates by \(\Sigma^{\star}+\xi\) and seek a formal coefficient vector
\[
 v(\xi)=v_0+\sum_{r\geq1}v_r(\xi),
\]
where \(v=(a,c,z)\) and \(v_r\) is homogeneous of degree \(r\) in the independent covariance increments \(\xi\).  At degree \(r\), the residual equations have the form
\[
 J(v_0)v_r=-R_r\bigl(\xi,v_1,\ldots,v_{r-1}\bigr),
\tag{10}
\]
where \(J(v_0)\) is the residual Jacobian and the right side is already determined.  Equation (6) makes \(J(v_0)\) invertible, so (10) recursively determines a unique \(v_r\) at every order.  If a covariance polynomial vanished on the incidence image, substitution into any such formal section would give that polynomial evaluated at \(\Sigma^{\star}+\xi\) as the zero formal series.  Algebraic independence of the entries of \(\xi\) then forces the polynomial itself to be zero.  Hence \(P_G=(0)\), the covariance projection is dominant, and (9) makes \(L/K_G\) finite.

The \(2^d\) formal sections lie over the common embedded covariance field
\(
 K_G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C[[\xi]]
\)
and their \(z_1\)-series are distinct because their constant terms are distinct.  If the minimal polynomial of \(z_1\) over \(K_G\) had degree smaller than \(2^d\), its image in \(\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C[[\xi]][t]\) would have more distinct roots than its degree, which is impossible over a field.  Therefore
\[
 [K_G(z_1):K_G]\geq2^d.
\tag{11}
\]
The multihomogeneous count (8) gives \([L:K_G]\leq2^d\), so (11) forces
\[
 [K_G(z_1):K_G]=[L:K_G]=2^d.
\tag{12}
\]
Equivalently, the original coefficient \(e^{\star}=P_1\to h\) separates every generic branch.  Since the extension has characteristic zero, its minimal polynomial is separable.  Clearing its coefficient denominators and removing the nonzero discriminant, the residual Jacobian determinant, and the relevant leading coefficients leaves a nonempty Zariski-open covariance set on which the \(2^d\) queried values remain distinct.

Now append one of the fully bidirected children \(w\) of \(0\) specified in \(\mathrm{def:attaining\mbox{-}family}\), put \(x_w=\lambda_{0w}\), and let \(z_w\) collect the new covariance row \((\sigma_{iw}:i\in V)\) and \(\sigma_{ww}\).  There is no new missing-bidirected residual involving \(w\).  For fixed old source coordinates and \(x_w\), the covariance congruence is a triangular polynomial change, with polynomial inverse, between the newly allowed disturbance coordinates and \(z_w\).  If \(L_0,K_0\) are the old fields, the new fields therefore satisfy
\[
 L_1=L_0(x_w,z_w),\qquad K_1=K_0(z_w),
\tag{13}
\]
and the entries of \(z_w\) are algebraically independent over \(L_0(x_w)\).  If \(u_1,\ldots,u_{2^d}\) is a \(K_0\)-basis of \(K_0(z_1)\), a relation
\(
 \sum_j r_j(z_w)u_j=0
\)
over \(K_0(z_w)\), after clearing denominators and comparing coefficients of the algebraically independent monomials in \(z_w\), would be a \(K_0\)-linear relation among the \(u_j\).  Thus all \(r_j\) vanish; the same basis spans after adjoining \(z_w\).  Consequently
\[
 [K_1(z_1):K_1]=[K_0(z_1):K_0]=2^d.
\tag{14}
\]
Iteration proves \(d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{k,n})=2^{k+1}\) for every \(n\geq2k+4\).

Finally, \(d=k+1\geq1\) and \(n-2\geq2d\), so
\(
 \binom{n-2}{2}\geq\binom{2d}{2}=d(2d-1)\geq d
\).
Thus \(\mathrm{thm:orientation\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}bound}\) gives \(D_k(n)\leq2^{k+1}\) throughout this regime, whereas the constructed member gives the reverse inequality.  Hence
\[
 D_k(n)=2^{k+1}\qquad(n\geq2k+4),
\]
with the asserted nonempty open separation set.
body.justification: A uniform attaining region turns the exponent from a loose Bezout count into a sharp coordinate frontier for a substantial size range.
body.gap: Foygel, Draisma, and Drton already exhibit cubic and quartic behavior in small SEMs, but not an all-\(k\) family with one edge separating \(2^{k+1}\) generic branches.
body.consumer: Software maintainers obtain adversarial benchmark families and users obtain a worst-case ambiguity warning indexed by the number of added parents.
